query_text: how do bacteriophages differ from antibiotics

content.text:
Bacteriophages (“phages”) and antibiotics both can be used against bacterial infections, but they work very differently.

| Feature | Bacteriophages | Antibiotics |
|---|---|---|
| **What they are** | Viruses that infect bacteria | Chemical drugs that inhibit or kill bacteria |
| **Target range** | Usually very specific — often one bacterial species or strain | Often broader — may affect many bacterial species |
| **How they work** | Attach to bacteria, inject genetic material, replicate, and often burst the bacterial cell | Interfere with bacterial processes like cell-wall synthesis, protein synthesis, DNA replication, or metabolism |
| **Effect on microbiome** | Typically less disruptive because they target specific bacteria | Can disrupt normal beneficial bacteria, especially broad-spectrum antibiotics |
| **Resistance** | Bacteria can become resistant to phages, but phages can also evolve alongside bacteria | Bacteria can become antibiotic-resistant; resistance can spread between bacteria |
| **Dosing behavior** | Can multiply at the infection site if susceptible bacteria are present | Do not replicate; drug levels depend on dose, absorption, metabolism, and clearance |
| **Use in medicine** | Used in some places and increasingly studied, especially for antibiotic-resistant infections | Widely used and standardized in modern medicine |
| **Regulation/standardization** | More complex because phages are biological and often tailored to the bacterial strain | Generally easier to manufacture and regulate as defined chemical compounds |

**In short:**  
Antibiotics are chemical treatments that often act broadly against bacteria, while bacteriophages are bacteria-infecting viruses that usually target very specific bacteria. Phages may be useful when bacteria are resistant to antibiotics, but they require careful matching to the infection-causing strain.
